verses.t: Mencius said, "Bo Yi would not let his eyes look on an evil sight, nor his ears listen to an evil sound. He would not serve a ruler who was not his proper ruler, nor command a people who were not his proper people. When there was good order he came forward; when there was disorder he withdrew. Where lawless government was carried on and lawless people lived, he could not bear to dwell. To be in the company of village folk seemed to him like sitting in court robes and court cap in mud and soot. In the time of Zhou [the tyrant] he lived on the shore of the Northern Sea, waiting for the world to become clean. So when people hear of the character of Bo Yi, the grasping man becomes clean-handed and the weak man gains a resolute will. Yi Yin said, 'Whom may I not serve as my ruler? Whom may I not command as my people?' He came forward in times of order, and came forward in times of disorder too. He said, 'Heaven, in producing this people, appointed those who first know to awaken those who know later, and those who are first awakened to awaken those who are awakened later. I am one of Heaven's people who has been awakened first; I will take this Way and awaken this people with it.' He thought that if among all the people under Heaven there was a single common man or woman who did not share in the blessings of Yao and Shun, it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch. Such was the weight of the world that he took upon himself. Liuxia Hui was not ashamed to serve a corrupt ruler, nor did he decline a small office. When he came forward he did not hide his worth, but always acted according to his Way. When he was dismissed and neglected he did not complain; when he was in distress and poverty he did not grieve. In the company of village folk he was easy and content and could not bear to leave them. 'You are you and I am I. Even if you stand beside me bare-armed and naked, how can you defile me?' So when people hear of the character of Liuxia Hui, the mean man becomes generous and the shallow man becomes sincere. When Confucius left Qi, he took up the rice he had been rinsing and set off at once. When he left Lu he said, 'Slowly, slowly I go; this is the way to leave the state of one's father and mother.' To hurry when it was right to hurry, to stay long when it was right to stay long, to remain out of office when it was right to remain out, to take office when it was right to take office: that was Confucius." Mencius said, "Bo Yi was the pure one among the sages; Yi Yin was the responsible one among the sages; Liuxia Hui was the accommodating one among the sages; Confucius was the timely one among the sages. Confucius is what we call the complete gathering of all. This gathering of all is like a performance in which the bronze bell opens and the jade stone concludes. The bronze bell sounds the beginning of the orderly sequence; the jade stone sounds its close. Beginning the orderly sequence is the work of wisdom; completing it is the work of sageliness. Wisdom may be compared to skill, and sageliness to strength. It is like shooting at a mark a hundred paces away: that your arrow reaches it is due to your strength, but that it hits the center is not due to your strength."

Beigong Qi asked, "How did the house of Zhou arrange its ranks and emoluments?" Mencius said, "The details cannot be learned, for the feudal lords, disliking them as harmful to themselves, have all done away with the records. Still, I have heard the general outline. The Son of Heaven was one rank, a duke one rank, a marquis one rank, an earl one rank, and a viscount and a baron together one rank: five grades in all. Within a state, the ruler was one rank, the minister one rank, the great officer one rank, the upper scholar-officer one rank, the middle scholar-officer one rank, and the lower scholar-officer one rank: six grades in all. By the regulations, the Son of Heaven held territory a thousand li square; dukes and marquises each held a hundred li square, earls seventy li, and viscounts and barons fifty li: four grades in all. Those whose land did not amount to fifty li had no direct access to the Son of Heaven but were attached to some feudal lord, and were called dependencies. The ministers of the Son of Heaven received land equal to a marquis, his great officers land equal to an earl, and his chief scholar-officers land equal to a viscount or baron. In a great state of a hundred li square, the ruler had ten times the emolument of a minister; a minister four times that of a great officer; a great officer twice that of an upper scholar-officer; an upper scholar-officer twice that of a middle one; a middle scholar-officer twice that of a lower one; and the lower scholar-officer the same as common people serving in office, an emolument enough to take the place of what they would have earned by farming. In a state of the next size, seventy li square, the ruler had ten times the emolument of a minister; a minister three times that of a great officer; a great officer twice that of an upper scholar-officer; an upper scholar-officer twice that of a middle one; a middle scholar-officer twice that of a lower one; and the lower scholar-officer the same as common people serving in office, enough to take the place of their farming. In a small state of fifty li square, the ruler had ten times the emolument of a minister; a minister twice that of a great officer; a great officer twice that of an upper scholar-officer; an upper scholar-officer twice that of a middle one; a middle scholar-officer twice that of a lower one; and the lower scholar-officer the same as common people serving in office, enough to take the place of their farming. As for what the farmers obtained, each husbandman received a hundred mu. With a hundred mu manured, the best farmers could feed nine people, the next best eight, the middling seven, the next six, and the lowest five. The emoluments of common people serving in office were graded on this scale."

Wan Zhang asked, "May I ask about friendship?" Mencius said, "Make friends without presuming on your age, without presuming on your rank, and without presuming on your brothers. To befriend someone is to befriend his virtue, and there must be no presuming on anything. Meng Xianzi was the head of a family of a hundred chariots, and he had five friends: Yuezheng Qiu, Mu Zhong, and three others whose names I have forgotten. When Xianzi was friends with these five, they took no account of his family. Had they taken account of his family, he would not have been friends with them. Not only the head of a family of a hundred chariots acted in this way; even the ruler of a small state did so. Duke Hui of Bi said, 'Zisi I treat as my teacher; Yan Ban I treat as my friend; Wang Shun and Chang Xi are men who serve me.' Not only the ruler of a small state acted in this way; even the ruler of a great state did so. Duke Ping of Jin, with Hai Tang, went in when told to go in, sat when told to sit, and ate when told to eat. Even if it was coarse rice and vegetable broth, he never failed to eat his fill, for he did not dare do otherwise. But it went no further than that. He did not share with him any of Heaven's positions, nor have him govern any of Heaven's offices, nor let him eat any of Heaven's emoluments. That was the way a scholar honors a worthy man, not the way a king or duke honors a worthy man. When Shun went up to see the Emperor [Yao], the Emperor lodged his son-in-law in a second palace and also dined with him, the two of them by turns host and guest. That was the Son of Heaven befriending a common man. When an inferior shows respect to a superior, it is called honoring the honorable; when a superior shows respect to an inferior, it is called esteeming the worthy. Honoring the honorable and esteeming the worthy rest on one and the same principle."

Wan Zhang asked, "May I ask what feeling should govern the giving and receiving of gifts?" Mencius said, "Respect." "Why is it that to decline them, and decline them again, is considered disrespectful?" "When an honored person gives you something, if you ask yourself, 'Was the way he got this right or not right?' and only then accept it, that is considered disrespectful. So one does not decline." Wan Zhang said, "Suppose I do not decline it in words, but decline it in my heart, saying to myself, 'He took this from the people unjustly,' and then refuse it on some other pretext. Would that not do?" Mencius said, "If he offers it on proper grounds and presents it with proper ceremony, then even Confucius would have accepted it." Wan Zhang said, "Suppose there is a man who waylays people outside the city gates, and he offers his gift on proper grounds and presents it with proper ceremony. Could one accept such plunder?" "No. The Announcement to Kang says, 'Those who kill men and overthrow them to take their goods, reckless and unafraid of death, are abhorred by all the people.' Such men are to be put to death without waiting for any instruction. This rule Yin received from Xia and Zhou received from Yin without question, and it is in force today with full strength. How could one accept such a gift?" Wan Zhang said, "The feudal lords of today take from the people just as a robber does. Yet if they observe the proper ceremonies, the gentleman accepts their gifts. May I ask how you explain this?" Mencius said, "Do you think that if a true king arose, he would round up all the feudal lords of today and put them to death? Or would he first instruct them, and put them to death only if they did not change? To say that anyone who takes what is not his own is a robber is to push a principle by analogy to its extreme. When Confucius held office in Lu, the people of Lu competed over the game taken in the hunt, and Confucius also competed. If even competing over the game was permissible, how much more accepting gifts!" Wan Zhang said, "Then when Confucius held office, was it not to carry out the Way?" "It was to carry out the Way." "If he was carrying out the Way, why did he compete over the game?" "Confucius first set down in writing the proper vessels for the sacrifices, and did not allow food gathered from all quarters to be offered in them." "Why did he not leave?" "He wished to make a trial. When the trial showed that the Way could be carried out and still it was not carried out, then he left. So he never stayed anywhere for three full years. Confucius took office sometimes because he saw that the Way might be practiced, sometimes because he was received with courtesy, and sometimes because the ruler wished to maintain worthy men. With Ji Huanzi, he took office because he saw the Way might be practiced; with Duke Ling of Wei, because he was received with courtesy; with Duke Xiao of Wei, because the ruler maintained worthy men."

Mencius said, "One takes office not because of poverty, yet there are times when one does so because of poverty. One marries a wife not to be supported, yet there are times when one does so to be supported. One who takes office because of poverty should decline a high position and occupy a low one, decline riches and accept a meager salary. Declining a high position for a low one, declining riches for a meager salary, what post is suitable? Guarding a gate or beating the watchman's rattle. Confucius once served as keeper of granaries, and said, 'My accounts must be correct, that is all.' He once served as keeper of the herds, and said, 'The oxen and sheep must grow strong and fat, that is all.' To speak of lofty matters when one's position is low is an offense; to stand in a ruler's court and not see the Way carried out is a disgrace."

Wan Zhang said, "Why is it that a scholar does not live as a dependent of a feudal lord?" Mencius said, "He does not presume to. When a feudal lord has lost his state and then lives as a dependent of another lord, that accords with ritual. For a scholar to live as a dependent of a feudal lord does not accord with ritual." Wan Zhang said, "If the ruler sends him grain, does he accept it?" "He accepts it." "On what principle does he accept it?" "A ruler is bound to relieve the needs of the common people." "Why is it that he accepts it as relief but will not accept it as a gift?" "He does not presume to." "May I ask why he does not presume to?" "Even the gatekeeper and the watchman have their regular duties for which they are fed by their superiors. To receive gifts from a superior without having regular duties is considered disrespectful." "If the ruler sends him gifts and he accepts them, may this be continued regularly?" "Duke Mu often sent to ask after Zisi and often sent him gifts of cooked meat. Zisi was displeased. At last he waved the messenger out of the great gate, bowed his head to the ground twice facing north, and declined the gift, saying, 'From now on I know that the ruler keeps me, Ji, as he keeps his dogs and horses.' After that no more gifts were sent from the servants. If one delights in worthy men but can neither raise them to office nor support them properly, can one be said to delight in worthy men?" "May I ask how the ruler of a state who wishes to support a gentleman should do it so that it may be called proper support?" "The first gift is presented by the ruler's command, and the gentleman receives it with two bows and his head to the ground. After that the granary keeper continues to supply grain and the cook continues to supply meat, without its being presented by the ruler's command. Zisi considered that the cooked meat made him bob up and down bowing again and again, and that this was not the way to support a gentleman. Yao, with Shun, had his nine sons serve him and gave him his two daughters in marriage, and supplied him with all the officials, oxen and sheep, granaries and storehouses, to support Shun in the midst of the fields, and afterward raised him to the highest place. Hence it is said, 'This is how a king or duke honors a worthy man.'"

Wan Zhang said, "May I ask on what principle you do not go to see the feudal lords?" Mencius said, "One living in the capital is called a subject of the marketplace and the well; one living in the countryside is called a subject of the grass and thickets. Both are called common people. It is the rule of ritual that common people who have not presented their token of introduction and become ministers do not presume to see a feudal lord." Wan Zhang said, "When a common man is summoned to perform labor service, he goes and serves. Yet when a ruler wishes to see him and summons him, he will not go to see him. Why is that?" "To go and serve is right; to go and see him is not right. Besides, why does the ruler wish to see him?" "Because of his wide learning, or because of his worth." "If it is because of his wide learning, even the Son of Heaven does not summon his teacher, much less a feudal lord. If it is because of his worth, I have never heard of anyone wishing to see a worthy man and summoning him. Duke Mu often visited Zisi and said, 'In ancient times, rulers of states of a thousand chariots made friends with scholars. What do you think of that?' Zisi was displeased and said, 'The ancients had a saying: one should serve him; did they ever say one should befriend him?' When Zisi was displeased, was he not saying, 'In terms of rank, you are the ruler and I am the subject; how could I presume to be the friend of my ruler? In terms of virtue, you are the one who should serve me; how could you be my friend?' If the ruler of a thousand chariots sought to be his friend and could not attain it, how much less could he summon him! Duke Jing of Qi, when hunting, summoned his gamekeeper with a pennon. The gamekeeper did not come, and the duke was going to have him killed. 'The resolute scholar does not forget that he may end in a ditch; the brave scholar does not forget that he may lose his head.' What did Confucius approve in him? He approved that he would not answer a summons that was not the proper one for him." "May I ask what should be used to summon a gamekeeper?" "A leather cap. A common man is summoned with a plain silk banner, a scholar with a banner bearing dragons, and a great officer with a feathered pennon. When a gamekeeper was summoned with the summons for a great officer, he would rather die than presume to go. If a common man were summoned with the summons for a scholar, how would he dare go? How much more when a worthy man is summoned with the summons for an unworthy one! To wish to see a worthy man and not go about it in the proper way is like wishing him to come in and shutting the door on him. Righteousness is the road and ritual is the door. Only the gentleman can follow this road and go in and out by this door. The Ode says, 'The road of Zhou is smooth as a whetstone, and straight as an arrow; the gentleman walks upon it, and the common people look on.'" Wan Zhang said, "When Confucius was summoned by his ruler's command, he set off without waiting for his carriage to be yoked. Was Confucius wrong, then?" "Confucius was in office and had official duties, and he was summoned in connection with his office."

Mencius said to Wan Zhang, "The finest scholar of a village will make friends with the finest scholars of the village; the finest scholar of a state will make friends with the finest scholars of the state; the finest scholar in the world will make friends with the finest scholars in the world. And if he finds that befriending the finest scholars in the world is not enough, he goes further and considers the people of ancient times. He recites their odes and reads their books; but can he do so without knowing what kind of men they were? So he considers the times they lived in. This is going back in time to make friends."

King Xuan of Qi asked about high ministers. Mencius said, "Which kind of high minister is Your Majesty asking about?" The king said, "Are they not all the same?" "They are not the same. There are high ministers who are of the ruler's own kin, and high ministers of a different surname." The king said, "May I ask about high ministers who are of the ruler's kin?" "If the ruler has great faults, they remonstrate with him; if after they have done so again and again he will not listen, they replace him." The king suddenly changed color. Mencius said, "Let Your Majesty not be surprised. Your Majesty asked me, and I dared not answer except truthfully." When the king's color had settled, he asked about high ministers of a different surname. Mencius said, "If the ruler has faults, they remonstrate with him; if after they have done so again and again he will not listen, they leave."
